data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: RxERP Outlines What the FDA’s Move to 12-Digit NDCs Means for Pharma Product Data
data.description:
New overview and checklist help teams review product matching, barcode data, and trading-partner workflows ahead of the 2033 change

ST. GEORGE, Utah--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- RxERP, the serialized enterprise resource planning platform purpose-built for the pharmaceutical supply chain, today released a 12-Digit NDC readiness overview and companion checklist to help pharmaceutical companies prepare their product records and workflows for the FDA’s new 12-digit NDC format. The resources build on RxERP’s support for 10-, 11-, and 12-digit representations of a product’s NDC within one product record, helping manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors, and 3PLs keep product identity consistent as formats change.

The operational challenge begins when trading partners identify the same product differently. A supplier’s code may fail to match the version stored in the receiving system, requiring a manual lookup or prompting creation of a duplicate item. Those duplicates can split inventory counts, lot history, and pricing across records. Adding a new NDC format makes reliable product matching essential across receiving, inventory, orders, and traceability data.

Under the FDA’s final rule, the uniform 12-digit NDC takes effect March 7, 2033, with a labeling transition through March 6, 2036. The rule itself leaves HIPAA standards unchanged, while the FDA expects billing standards to accommodate 12 digits by 2033.

The transition also changes how systems connect National Drug Codes with Global Trade Item Numbers, or GTINs, used in serialized workflows. The existing NDC-based GTIN structure cannot embed a 12-digit NDC. Software that extracts an NDC from a GTIN will therefore need to change how it associates the identifiers with the correct product and packaging level. GS1 application identifier 715 provides a way to carry the NDC as a separate barcode data element alongside the GTIN.

“A product shouldn’t become two products because a trading partner sent its NDC in a different format,” said Steve Madsen, founder and CEO of RxERP. “We connect those NDC formats to one product record so teams can maintain a consistent product identity. These resources help companies identify the remaining work across barcodes, integrations, and trading partners while they have time to plan and test.”

The overview explains the conversion rules, the GTIN mapping challenge, and actions for manufacturers, repackagers, distributors, 3PLs, and pharmacies. The companion checklist turns that guidance into a working assessment, with space to record test results, document evidence, assign owners, and set follow-up dates. Teams can use it to test whether their systems can:

  • Match original and converted NDCs to the correct product and package record while preserving strength, dosage form, and package differences.
  • Preserve leading zeros and handle newly assigned 12-digit NDCs without misclassifying them as UPCs.
  • Interpret GS1 AI (715) through both the scanner and receiving application while continuing to process existing barcodes.
  • Exchange identifiers correctly with trading partners and follow a product through receiving, inventory, an outbound order, and serialized-data workflows.

RxERP brings product records, serialized data, inventory, and orders into the same platform, with serialization built into operational workflows. Its FDA NDC API integration brings FDA product data into the item master, and product setup draws on FDA and GS1 data to reduce manual entry. Keeping NDC representations associated with one product record provides a foundation for the broader barcode and trading-partner work required by the transition.

Read the 12-Digit NDC overview and download the working checklist at https://rxerp.com/12-digit-ndc-transition/

About RxERP

RxERP is a purpose-built, fully serialized pharmaceutical ERP that unifies financial management, inventory, distribution, warehouse operations, customer ordering, DSCSA compliance, and EPCIS traceability within one integrated platform. RxERP helps pharmaceutical manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors, 3PL providers, and pharmacies expanding into distribution streamline operations, to reduce manual processes, support compliance workflows, and scale with greater visibility and control. Learn more at rxerp.com.

data.title: GTCR explores potential takeover of payments firm Global Payments
data.description:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - GTCR is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments ( GPN ), the private equity group said in a filing on Friday, days after reports that a consortium effort with CD&R was dropped.

Shares of Global Payments ( GPN ) closed the day 10% higher. It was up about 19% so far in 2026.

GTCR is working with other private equity firms to finance the potential deal, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. GTCR, which holds a 16.35% stake in Global Payments ( GPN ) and is the largest shareholder, said no definitive decision has been made.

Global Payments ( GPN ) did not immediately respond to Reuters request for a comment.

Private equity firms CD&R and GTCR had dropped their pursuit of Global Payments ( GPN ) as a buyout consortium, Reuters reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter.

The report had added that it was possible that CD&R and GTCR will resume the talks with Global Payments ( GPN ) at a later date or another buyer for the company may emerge.

Atlanta-based Global Payments ( GPN ) is one of the world's largest payment processors. It enables merchants to accept card and digital payments and provides software and technology services to businesses. Its market value stood at about $22 billion, as of last close.

The company has faced pressure in recent years from slowing growth in some business lines, intensifying competition and investor demands to boost profitability.

Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover deal first and said it could value Global Payments ( GPN ) at $50 billion, including debt and premium.

(Reporting by Pritam Biswas in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)

data.title: Exclusive-Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium to accept US takeover, documents and source say
data.description:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant that the company would not own or control, according to documents reviewed by Reuters and a person with direct knowledge of the request.

The company rejected the proposal, saying such a stake would likely garner public scrutiny, risk future capital-raising and outweigh any benefit to shareholders, the documents from July and August showed.  

"51% is far outside precedent and invites scrutiny," Pure Lithium's legal counsel Skadden Arps wrote in an August 22 memorandum reviewed by Reuters that outlined Lutnick's request.

The federal government's unsuccessful attempt to take majority control of Pure Lithium has not been previously reported.

This article is based on documents that include emails between Pure Lithium and the Commerce Department discussing a meeting between Lutnick and Pure Lithium's CEO, as well as a memorandum written by Pure Lithium's legal counsel outlining Lutnick's request.

Lutnick's plan marks one of the latest moves by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company and comes as the secretary and former investment banker faces increased scrutiny over his ties to corporate executives and companies affected by decisions made by his department.

The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including chipmaker Intel, extending its reach into the private sector in a way recent administrations have not.

However, it has not taken a majority stake in any company, with its most serious effort a proposed rescue of Spirit Airlines, the low-budget airline that ceased operations in May. Thus far, the largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials, which would make it the largest shareholder.

A Pure Lithium representative, when asked about the proposal, did not dispute the account.

The Commerce Department did not respond to questions about the proposal posed by Reuters for this story.

It is not illegal for the federal government to acquire equity stakes in a private company and the administration has defended these efforts, particularly through using funds stemming from 2022's CHIPS Act, which was designed to boost domestic research and manufacturing of semiconductors. 

Lawmakers opposed to the practice, though, contend the law never authorized such ownership. No court has ruled on the question. 

Privately held Pure Lithium has developed a lithium metal battery that it says is far more efficient than a traditional lithium-ion battery and can be built without graphite, nickel or cobalt.

If Pure Lithium's battery can deliver, it would be a major advancement for the energy storage industry. If mass produced, the battery could potentially shift how the US military and other federal contractors power millions of devices, analysts have said. 

At a July 29 meeting in Washington with Pure Lithium CEO Emilie Bodoin, Lutnick expressed interest in the battery's capabilities, including its efficiency. He said the US government needed to control the company so the battery could be used by the US military and other agencies, according to the person and documents reviewed by Reuters.

The two had been meeting to discuss a legal dispute with Japan's Panasonic related to the battery technology, according to the person and the documents. 

The meeting, which lasted roughly 45 minutes, was arranged by billionaire Robert Friedland, one of Pure Lithium's largest shareholders. A company co-founded by Friedland, I-Pulse, received $250 million from the Commerce Department in June. 

Friedland attended the July meeting alongside David Shapiro, a senior adviser at the Commerce Department, according to the documents. Through a spokesperson, Friedland declined to comment for this article.

The White House has repeatedly said strategic investments in the minerals and related sectors are needed because they are critical to US economic competitiveness. The White House did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Reuters has no evidence that Lutnick personally holds a stake in either I-Pulse or Pure Lithium. A Commerce Department spokesperson, speaking on behalf of Lutnick, said she did not think he is invested in either company. Both companies are privately held and do not need to disclose their ownership. 

US CONTROL DISCUSSED

As part of his effort to persuade Bodoin to give the government the controlling stake, Lutnick said the takeover could also help with the Panasonic dispute, according to the person. Pure Lithium sued Panasonic in March, accusing the Japanese company of reverse-engineering Pure Lithium's lithium metal battery technology, an allegation Panasonic disputes. The case is set for a January hearing to decide whether to grant Pure Lithium a preliminary injunction against Panasonic.

The Commerce chief had previously helped negotiate a tariff-linked agreement last year that included a $550 billion pledge from Tokyo to invest in the US economy. 

In exchange for the majority stake, Lutnick said that $1 billion from Japan's pledge would be set aside to build a manufacturing plant that a special-purpose investment vehicle controlled by Tokyo and Washington would own, according to an August 22 memo from Pure Lithium's attorneys to Friedland. 

However, Pure Lithium would not have received any funding under the proposal, according to the documents. The company would have been contracted to operate but not own the plant, and would be granted a portion of the plant's revenue after paying for the debt servicing costs on the invested $1 billion.

Lutnick also told Pure Lithium to send 100 of its batteries to the Energy and Defense departments for testing, according to the documents.

Pure Lithium rejected Lutnick's requests, citing the lack of funds in the proposal for the company and expected public scrutiny, saying such an arrangement would "cripple Pure Lithium's ability to raise capital or pursue an IPO," according to the memorandum written by Pure Lithium's counsel Skadden Arps, which objected because Pure Lithium would not have control of the proposed manufacturing plant.

The Commerce Department rejected Pure Lithium's 9.9% counterproposal in August.

"Commerce remains fixed on 51% equity in Pure Lithium," said the August 22 memo from Pure Lithium's attorneys to Friedland. The Commerce Department "is prepared to move on to other projects if Pure Lithium does not meet the mark."

Lutnick has boosted the Commerce Department's investments in the minerals sector as part of a plan first reported by Reuters last year to reallocate funding approved in the 2022 CHIPS Act for semiconductor research and factory construction. 

Those interests include stakes in USA Rare Earth and Korea Zinc, while other federal agencies have taken stakes in different mining companies.

(Reporting by Ernest Scheyder; additional reporting by Jan Wolfe in New York; editing by Veronica Brown and David Gaffen)

data.title: fraud0 Partners with FouAnalytics to Offer Impression-Level Digital Media Governance - to Replace DoubleVerify and IAS
data.description:
Advertisers get every impression measured by FouAnalytics, humans and bots both counted, and wasted spend recovered through fraud0 Google Ads refunds

NEW YORK and MUNICH , Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- fraud0, the company behind the AI agent for Google Ads refunds, today announced a further partnership with FouAnalytics, the independent analytics platform for digital ads, websites and mobile apps. This partnership builds on the companies' earlier agreement to offer Google Ads refunds to advertisers. It lets fraud0 customers use FouAnalytics impression-level measurement as their digital media governance system, replacing legacy verification vendors such as DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science (IAS).

For more than a decade, legacy verification reports have told advertisers that invalid traffic (IVT) was around 1% and that their campaigns were 99% "fraud free." Independent audits have consistently found much higher levels of fraud and waste. Today, even advertisers no longer believe these low IVT numbers from the legacy vendors, and many are looking for an independent way to see what is really happening in their campaigns.

FouAnalytics was built to give them that view. It measures every ad impression and collects 300 to 500 parameters for each one. The platform is deterministic, not probabilistic. It uses red flags to mark automation and blue flags to mark real human interaction, such as mouse movements, scrolling and touch events. Because it positively measures for humans, not just bots, advertisers have two levers to pull. They can cut off sources of fraud (less red, bots) and shift budget toward sites and apps that reach more real people (more blue, humans). FouAnalytics also detects other forms of waste, like ad stacking, pixel stuffing, made-for-advertising (MFA) sites, ad slot refreshing and forced redirects.

FouAnalytics in-ad tags fire after the ad has rendered, so they record where the ad actually ran, not just what the bid request claimed. This matters because fraudulent sites routinely put reputable domains in their bid requests to win bids. Log-level data repeats those false domains, which lets fraud and MFA sites disappear from reports. FouAnalytics impression-level data shows where the ads really went. Advertisers can then compare bids won, ads served and ads actually rendered.

The FouAnalytics dashboard summarizes and labels impression-level data so executives can act on it quickly, without needing data scientists to process billions of rows of log files. If a third of impressions in a month are marked dark red, advertisers know right away which bad sites and apps to add to block lists. Setup takes minutes -- advertisers just copy and paste FouAnalytics in-ad tags into their DSP or ad server.

FouAnalytics also has cybersecurity built in. Every tag is unique and single-use, and its code is obfuscated, so bad actors can't tamper with measurement or test their bots against detection. The platform is privacy-compliant by design. It never collects personally identifiable information, never sets cookies, and keeps EU data in its Frankfurt data center, and IP addresses are discarded.

The partnership gives advertisers a complete governance loop. FouAnalytics shows them, impression by impression, where their money went and whether real humans saw their ads. fraud0 then analyzes invalid clicks, bots, billing anomalies, overdelivery and traffic outside targeted regions, then builds the evidence and manages refund claims with Google. Approved refunds are credited back to the advertiser's Google Ads account.

"Legacy verification was designed to reassure advertisers, not to protect them," said Dr. Augustine Fou, founder and CEO of FouAnalytics. "FouAnalytics measures every impression so advertisers can 'see Fou themselves' where their ads went and whether humans saw them. Paired with fraud0's refund capabilities, advertisers can now find the waste and get the money back. That is real governance, not transparency theater."

"We see far too many bot clicks in display campaigns,just like with other types of campaigns," said Tilman Pfeiffer, CEO of fraud0. "Now we can finally give our customers the placement-level data to identify and remove this wasted spend"

Advertisers interested in replacing legacy verification with impression-level governance and automated Google Ads refunds can contact fraud0 or FouAnalytics.

Its privacy-friendly technology helps companies eliminate fraudulent traffic, protect ad spend, and improve marketing performance. More details at www.fraud0.com.

data.title: Methuselah Advisors Issues Open Letter to the Board of Directors of NVIDIA Corporation
data.description:
NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Methuselah Advisors today issued the following open letter:

To: Harvey C. Jones, Chairman, and the Board of Directors of NVIDIA Corporation

Re: The Removal of Jensen Huang — Fiduciary Responsibility, Shareholder Value, and the Imperative of Due Process

Dear Chairman Jones and Members of the Board:

The decision to separate Jensen Huang from NVIDIA, the company he founded and led for more than three decades represents, in our judgment, an extraordinary failure of corporate stewardship. It raises serious questions about whether NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has adequately discharged its fiduciary responsibilities to shareholders or has instead subordinated their economic interests to considerations of personal conduct, reputational sensitivity, and corporate virtue signaling.

The consequences have been staggering. NVIDIA has experienced a decline approaching 36% of its market capitalization during the controversy, representing more than $1.4 trillion dollars in lost shareholder value. While market movements reflect multiple influences, there can be little question that the abrupt displacement of the executive most closely identified with NVIDIA’s extraordinary success has introduced substantial uncertainty into the company’s future.

The Board has a responsibility to explain why such a consequential action was necessary before its own investigation had reached a publicly disclosed conclusion.

Let us begin with what is known.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged personal conduct that has become the subject of widespread public criticism. Reports of extramarital relationships, including one involving an individual suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence, understandably warrant careful review and scrutiny. Allegations involving relationships with company employees likewise merit examination under NVIDIA’s policies and established standards of corporate governance. Consenting adults or not, companies have HR policies and they apply all the way to the top.

We do not suggest that any chief executive, irrespective of accomplishment, should be exempt from accountability. Nor should national-security concerns, potential conflicts of interest, or violations of applicable law ever be minimized.

But there is a profound difference between conduct that warrants independent investigation and confirmed findings that justify the permanent removal of an extraordinarily successful chief executive.

Personal infidelity is not, by itself, evidence of corporate misconduct, a breach of fiduciary responsibility, or an inability to lead a public enterprise.

The relevant questions are whether Huang knowingly facilitated any unlawful transfer of NVIDIA technology, compromised proprietary information, violated applicable export restrictions, abused his corporate authority, or otherwise engaged in conduct materially detrimental to the company and its shareholders.

These questions demand a thorough, independent, evidence-based investigation. They cannot responsibly be answered through public speculation, moral condemnation, or an understandable desire to distance the corporation from an embarrassing controversy.

Indeed, on November 8, NVIDIA’s own Board publicly stated that it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised. It simultaneously expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.

Within days, that confidence had apparently evaporated.

What changed?

What evidence emerged between those statements and Huang’s departure that justified removing the individual most responsible for NVIDIA’s strategic leadership, technological dominance, commercial relationships, and extraordinary creation of shareholder wealth?

The Board has not adequately answered that question publicly.

Even more troubling is its subsequent declaration that Huang will not be reinstated as chief executive, notwithstanding the continuing investigation.

How can the Board have reached an apparently irrevocable judgment when the investigation intended to establish the underlying facts remains incomplete?

Corporate directors are not appointed to serve as arbiters of personal morality. They are entrusted with protecting the enterprise, exercising independent judgment, evaluating risk, complying with applicable law, and preserving and enhancing long-term shareholder value.

That responsibility necessarily encompasses appropriate standards of executive behavior. But it also requires proportionality, procedural rigor, and an understanding of the economic consequences of every major corporate decision.

NVIDIA is not an ordinary enterprise, and Jensen Huang is not an interchangeable executive.

Under his leadership, NVIDIA evolved from a graphics-chip company into the central technological infrastructure provider of the artificial-intelligence revolution. Its commercial architecture, developer ecosystem, strategic customer relationships, and leadership in accelerated computing are inseparable from the vision and execution he provided over more than three decades.

The company’s latest quarterly financial performance reinforces the magnitude of that achievement: revenue of $115.8 billion, an increase of 103% from the comparable period one year earlier.

Replacing the architect of that success is not analogous to replacing an executive in an established business operating within a mature and predictable industry.

It introduces consequential risks to strategy, innovation, customer relationships, employee confidence, geopolitical negotiations, and competitive positioning during one of the most important technological transitions in modern history. These risks must be weighed against the actual, demonstrable risks associated with Huang’s continued participation in the enterprise.

We are particularly troubled by the possibility that the Board has effectively substituted the appearance of moral rectitude for a considered economic and legal analysis of its responsibilities.

Corporate governance cannot become a contest in reputational purification, in which allegations of personal misconduct automatically outweigh decades of exceptional performance without a disciplined examination of their relevance to the business.

Shareholders are entitled to more. The massive destruction of value demands it. And there is a practical and responsible alternative.

We urge the Board to invite Jensen Huang to return immediately as Executive Chairman, pending completion of its independent investigation.

Under such an arrangement, he could continue providing strategic leadership, technical vision, continuity in key commercial relationships, and institutional knowledge, while Colette Kress and the existing management team retain responsibility for day-to-day operations.

The Board should with counsel establish clear and independently enforced safeguards, including appropriate restrictions on Huang’s involvement in any matter implicated by the investigation, relevant export-control decisions, and relationships that might create conflicts of interest.

The independent committee and its outside counsel must retain complete authority to investigate without interference. Any return to an executive position must also be consistent with applicable legal, regulatory, and national-security requirements.

This structure would allow NVIDIA to preserve the value of its founder’s leadership without compromising the integrity of the investigation.

At its conclusion, the Board should make a fully informed determination, grounded in verified evidence, as to whether Huang should resume the position of Chief Executive Officer, continue in another appropriate executive capacity, or permanently leave the company.

If material wrongdoing is established, appropriate action should follow. But if the investigation produces no substantiated finding of serious corporate misconduct, the Board should be prepared to restore Huang’s leadership rather than allow an extraordinary corporate achievement to be diminished by an exercise in reputational expediency.

We recognize that the Board may possess material nonpublic information that cannot presently be disclosed. If so, it must act consistently with its legal obligations and the integrity of the investigation. Nevertheless, shareholders deserve an explanation of the process employed, the alternatives considered, and the reasons an interim leadership arrangement involving Huang was rejected.

The Board should also explain how it assessed the enormous economic consequences of permanently severing NVIDIA’s relationship with its founder, particularly when the company was continuing to deliver exceptional financial and operating results.

It is not sufficient merely to express confidence in a successor management team or gratitude for Huang’s past contributions.

The obligation is to demonstrate that the decision to remove him permanently represents the best available course for the enterprise and its owners.

Fiduciary responsibility is not discharged by demonstrating moral disapproval. It is discharged by exercising informed, independent, proportionate judgment in the long-term interests of the corporation and its shareholders.

The Board’s handling of this episode has raised serious doubts about whether that standard has been met.

We therefore urge you to reconsider the decision not to reinstate Huang, establish a carefully controlled interim Executive Chairman arrangement, complete the independent investigation with dispatch, and defer any permanent determination concerning his future until the relevant facts are established.

NVIDIA’s shareholders should not be required to bear the potentially permanent economic consequences of a judgment that may have been rendered before the evidence was in.

There is still an opportunity for the Board to demonstrate sound judgment, restore confidence, and distinguish legitimate corporate accountability from unnecessary destruction of shareholder value.

We urge you to seize it.

Respectfully,

John Chachas
Co-Managing Partner
Methuselah Advisors

data.title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Tech leads global stocks rout, Treasury yields fall
data.description:
(Updates to US stock market close)

* Broad index of global stocks in biggest weekly drop since 2020

* Anthropic shares fall as much as 14.5% to just above IPO pricing

* US bonds rally, spot gold and silver at 14-month lows

* US chipmakers, Taiwan stocks each fall 17% for the week

By Rodrigo Campos

NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Tumbling technology-related shares led a global stock sell off on Friday, with US traders searching for safe havens as the US 10-year yield dropped by the most in a month.

Traders sold stocks in most markets with Japan and Korea down more than 5% overnight. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while on Wall Street chip-maker shares fell 10.7% Friday and 17.1% for the week.

Anthropic, which debuted this week, fell as much as 14.5% on its first full day of trading, just above its $83 IPO pricing, and ended down 9.1% at $88.30.

Consumer staples was the sole S&P 500 sector to end in the black on Friday.

"Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.

"Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the outlook for corporate profitability."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 34.89 points, or 3.30%, to 1,021.91. Its weekly decline of 8.1% was the largest since early 2020.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 2%, emerging market stocks fell 3.10% and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed lower by 3.27%. Japan's Nikkei fell 5.06%.

The VIX index, linked to the cost of insurance against a drop in the S&P 500, closed at its highest since April 2025.

As investors sought safe-haven assets, government bonds rallied.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 10.43 basis points to 4.948%, the largest daily drop since October 22. The 30-year bond yield fell 6.81 basis points to 5.3329%. The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, fell 13.21 basis points to 4.647% even as a rate hike is priced in for next month's policy meeting.

DOLLAR FLAT, OIL RISES LATE

The dollar index was little changed after touching a 19-month high on Thursday. The dollar's recent rally has been fueled by bets on tighter monetary policy due to hotter-than-expected US inflation data.

"I think the momentum has stalled for the dollar ... but I think it's a little bit early to pick a top for the dollar," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.

The dollar index fell 0.05% to 103.90, with the euro down 0.05% at $1.0961. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar weakened 0.67% to 158.6.

In commodities, crude prices rose late on Friday on worries about possible attacks in the US-Israeli war with Iran, and as traders bought crude ahead of next week's Thanksgiving holiday.

US crude rose 1.49% to $83.67 a barrel and Brent rose to $92.61 per barrel, up 0.68% on the day.

Gold prices fell to a 14-month low after the largest weekly drop in 8 months.

Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.09 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.22% to $40.95 an ounce. Copper declined 2.9% to $12,162.50 a ton.

(Reporting by Rodrigo Campos, Harry Robertson, Anna Hirtenstein, Saqib Iqbal Ahmed; editing by Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Nick Zieminski and Jonathan Spicer )

data.title: Update: AI Worries Send S&P 500 Into Correction Territory as Nasdaq Turns Negative For The Year
data.description:
05:15 PM EST, 11/20/2026 (MT Newswires) -- (Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered correction territory Friday, while the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year amid mounting skepticism around stocks linked to artificial intelligence.

The S&P 500 tumbled 3.7% to 6,910.39, extending its losing streak to a seventh consecutive session. The Dow dipped 1.9% to 48,147.33, marking its fifth day of decline.

A 10% stock pullback from recent highs is considered the minimum threshold for a market correction. Investors are concerned about the durability of the AI boom amid soaring valuations.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq plummeted 5.3% to 22,617.73, logging two back-to-back losses. The index is now down 2.7% this year.

Except consumer staples, all sectors ended in the red, led by tech's 7.1% slump.

This week, the Nasdaq shed 10%, while the S&P 500 slid 8.6%. The Dow recorded a weekly loss of 8%.

"The strength of the AI buildout has now spread wide enough that its end -- and we're certainly not saying that is now -- would likely trigger a broader bear market in equities, a downturn in the US economy and reversal of (Federal Reserve) policy," said Robert Kavcic, senior economist at BMO.

Anthropic's (ANT) shares tumbled 8.5%, having surged 17% in the previous session following a record Nasdaq debut. The Claude AI chatbot maker said Friday it completed its upsized initial public offering, raising about $93.5 billion.

"The ANT got squished (and) took the whole AI trade down with it," Scotiabank said in a note.

Tech bellwether Nvidia ( NVDA ) slid 14%, the worst performer on the Dow and among the steepest declines on the S&P 500. The Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Nvidia's ( NVDA ) accounting practices, Reuters reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.

Major chipmakers such as Intel ( INTC ) , Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) , Qualcomm ( QCOM ) , Micron Technology ( MU ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) fell sharply. Shares of AI hyperscalers including Microsoft ( MSFT ) , Amazon ( AMZN ) and Meta Platforms ( META ) also declined.

Treasury yields declined, with the two-year rate down 13 basis points at 4.65% and the 10-year rate falling 10.2 basis points to 4.95%.

Inflation in the US continues to be "unacceptably high" and the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike in September is unlikely to help ease price pressures, Fed Governor Lisa Cook said Friday.

US consumer sentiment improved in November, led by "substantial" increases in expected business conditions following the midterm elections, while the year-ahead inflation outlook reached its lowest level since February, a survey by the University of Michigan showed.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil edged up 0.9% to $83.98 a barrel, while Brent rose 0.6% to $92.50 a barrel.

China is set to overtake the US as the world's largest oil consumer by around 2034 as Washington navigates an economic slowdown and benefits from fuel efficiency gains, Oxford Economics said in a note.

Spot gold fell 2.4% to $3,538.49 per troy ounce, while silver shed 7.5% to $41.52 per ounce.

data.title: ASU still the No. 1 public school of choice for international students
data.description:
University rises to No. 2 among US public and private institutions, its highest-ever overall position in annual Open Doors report

TEMPE, Ariz., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For the sixth consecutive year, Arizona State University has been recognized as the No. 1 public university in the United States for hosting international students in the IIE 2026 Open Doors Report, ahead of the University of Illinois, Purdue University and the University of Michigan.

During the 2025–26 academic year, ASU was home to 20,926 international students, an increase of 2.7% from the previous year. The total, which includes enrolled international students and ASU graduates participating in Optional Practical Training programs, placed ASU No. 2 overall among all U.S. institutions for the first time in university history.

The milestone places ASU second only to New York University in the overall ranking and ahead of such institutions as Columbia University, the University of Southern California and Boston University.

ASU's achievement comes amid persistent visa delays and travel restrictions that have affected international enrollment at colleges and universities across the country. To address the concerns and uncertainty many international students faced about traveling to the U.S. for college, ASU enrollment teams work closely with prospective students and their families throughout the year, helping students understand their options, complete the enrollment process and begin their ASU experience.

Vianca Socolich Rivera, a biomedical sciences student in Barrett, The Honors College from Peru, was among the international students newly enrolled in the fall 2026 semester that ASU supported during her application process.

"Coming to the U.S. was always something I wanted to do, and even with all the uncertainty this year, I wasn't going to let that stop me," Rivera said. "I expected the visa process to be much harder, but ASU made sure I had the information and documents I needed to prepare.

A home away from home

See some of the dozens of celebrations, workshops and get-togethers — open to international and domestic students alike — that help students from other countries find community at ASU.

"I chose ASU because I saw how many international students were welcomed here, and I knew I would be part of a community with people from all over the world. I was also excited by ASU's innovation, research and opportunities in STEM. From the moment I arrived, the International Welcome event and the variety of student clubs made it much easier to adapt and feel like I belonged."

"Students like Vianca remind us of something very important," said Matt López, ASU vice president of enrollment. "Despite the persistent national narrative about declining international enrollment, there is no shortage of qualified, brilliant students around the world who want to be here. International students still see our institutions as keys to unlocking their potential."

"I am proud of our students for staying true to their goals, and proud of our team for working so hard to help them become Sun Devils."

Building on a decade of growth and impact

ASU first topped the Institute of International Education rankings for public universities in its 2014–15 report, when it hosted 11,300 international students. The university held that top spot in all but two subsequent years, during a decade in which its international student enrollment nearly doubled to 20,926 in 2025–26.

"The growth in our international student population has coincided with an explosion of demand for ASU across all student types," ASU President Michael Crow said.

"Because our charter requires an unyielding focus on accessible admissions practices and excellent academics, we have become a destination for the world's talent, enrolling record numbers of international students and Arizonans alike. When a university measures itself by whom it includes rather than priding itself on exclusivity, it creates an academic community with capacity for all qualified students."

The growth in international student enrollment has contributed to both the intellectual and cultural fabric of ASU as well as the economic vitality of Arizona. A 2025 analysis of the economic impact of ASU's international students found that their presence contributes nearly $700 million to Arizona's gross domestic product and supports almost 6,000 jobs for Arizonans.

Designing a global education for jobs of the future

ASU's global engagement extends beyond welcoming international students to its campuses. In the 2026 Open Doors report, ASU ranked No. 10 among U.S. institutions awarding credit for study abroad, with a university-record 2,852 students receiving credit for an international learning experience during the 2024–25 academic year.

ASU also ranked No. 9 among leading doctorate-focused institutions awarding credit for study abroad and No. 8 among doctorate-focused institutions for short-term study abroad, with 2,114 students participating in such programs.

"Together, our enrollment and study abroad rankings reflect ASU's design aspiration to engage globally," said Nancy Gonzales, executive vice president and university provost. "They provide evidence of the healthy flow of talent to and from our university, reaching almost every country in the world. Our responsibility now and into the future is to continue shaping the educational experiences on our campuses and through study abroad so that our students are prepared to succeed in a rapidly changing global economy."

One recent example of ASU's commitment to career-relevant study abroad is its new partnership with the Council on International Educational Exchange, which will launch the ASU Taiwan Internship Program in summer 2027.

Through the four-year initiative, an inaugural cohort of 55 undergraduate students will complete eight-week summer internships in Taiwan, gaining firsthand experience in a global workplace while building connections to Arizona's growing economic relationship with Taiwan.

The program is designed to prepare students for in-demand careers in fields including engineering, microelectronics, supply chain, international business, communications and sustainability. It builds on ASU's engagement with Taiwan as companies such as TSMC expand in Arizona, creating a model for study abroad that combines cultural learning with the professional skills and experience employers increasingly seek.

Ian Wei Xuen Foong, a newly enrolled computer systems engineering student from Malaysia, was drawn to ASU in part because of the access it offers students to companies such as TSMC.

"When I was deciding which university to attend, ASU was one of my choices because it is a large university with many opportunities for undergraduate students to gain practical experience," Foong said. "Its close connection to the semiconductor industry in Arizona also made me interested."

"Joining ASU will allow me to develop beyond my technical field in computer engineering and become a more well-rounded person in an ever-changing world. I want to return to my home country with not only technical knowledge but also the broader skills and perspectives needed to adapt to its changing job market."

While ASU anticipates that enrolling international students will remain challenging across higher education, its leaders remain optimistic and focused on making ASU a welcoming university home for all students.

"As much as we will continue to tell international students why coming to ASU will change their lives, our students always say it best," López said. "I'm reminded of Vianca's advice to future international students: 'Just be brave. Be bold. You have a community here for you.'"

data.title: US Transportation Dept watchdog to audit FAA oversight of Boeing
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Transportation Department Office of Inspector General said on Friday it will audit the Federal Aviation Administration's oversight of Boeing ( BA ) and other airplane manufacturers and aerospace suppliers.

The inspector general also wants to review a recent update to the FAA's risk assessment practices for overseeing manufacturers and the FAA's oversight of aircraft manufacturers' "quality assurance systems for domestic and foreign suppliers."

The watchdog noted that several reports have shown shortcomings in FAA and internal company oversight of Boeing's ( BA ) manufacturing processes. It cited a critical National Transportation Safety Board report into the mid-air cabin blowout of a new Alaska Airlines Boeing 737 MAX found ​missing four ⁠key bolts in January 2024.

It noted that the NTSB cited ineffective FAA oversight of Boeing ( BA ). An FAA spokesman said the agency welcomes feedback and will cooperate fully with the audit.

Boeing ( BA ) did not immediately comment.

The FAA said after the Alaska incident it "fundamentally changed how it oversees Boeing ( BA )" and for 21 months barred it from producing more than 38 737 MAX planes per month.

In September, the FAA disclosed Boeing ( BA ) had paid a $3.1 million fine after the agency said the ​planemaker had committed a series of safety violations, including some tied to ‌the 2024 Alaska Airlines incident.

The FAA also fined ​Boeing for interfering with safety officials' independence and said the planemaker presented ⁠for agency approval two aircraft that were not airworthy.

In 2024, the FAA said ​it found hundreds of quality system violations at the planemaker's 737 factory in Renton, ​Washington, and the 737 fuselage factory of then-Boeing ( BA ) subcontractor Spirit AeroSystems in Wichita, Kansas, from September 2023 through February 2024.

In recent months, the FAA has said Boeing ( BA ) has made significant improvements.

The FAA in July said it would allow ​Boeing to issue airworthiness certificates for all 737 MAX and 787 airplanes. The agency said the "decision follows months of thorough data and safety review demonstrating consistent production ​quality and reflects the FAA's confidence in Boeing's ( BA ) ability to issue airworthiness certificates ⁠under FAA oversight."

The FAA in recent months also certified the smaller MAX 7 and larger MAX 10 airplanes.

(Reporting by David Shepardson, Ryan Patrick Jones and Christian Martinez; Editing by Doina Chiacu and David Gregorio)

data.title: Oracle says OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after final capital raise

data.title: SUNation Energy Announces Third Quarter 2026 Results; Reports Sequential Revenue and Gross Margin Improvement and Provides Suniva Merger Update
data.description:
Third-quarter revenue of $11.2 million increased from $8.2 million in the second quarter; year-over-year results continued to reflect lower residential demand following the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit.

Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.7 million; SG&A expense declined 37% year-over-year to $4.3 million.

Results included $9.8 million of non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges.

SUNation continues to prioritize liquidity, cost management, and execution of its proposed merger with Suniva.

RONKONKOMA, N.Y., Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SUNation Energy, Inc. ( SUNE ) (“SUNation” or the “Company”), a leading provider of residential and commercial solar energy systems, battery storage solutions and comprehensive energy services, today announced financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 (“Q3 2026”).

Third-quarter revenue increased sequentially to $11.2 million from $8.2 million, and gross margin improved to 30.8% from 26.1%, reflecting higher revenue across the Company’s New York and Hawaii operations. Year-over-year performance continued to reflect downward pressure from the residential solar market’s adjustment to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (“OBBBA”). Consolidated revenue declined 41% year over year, with lower residential revenue partially offset by growth in commercial revenue.

SUNation Reduces Costs and Advances Suniva Merger

The Company continued to manage its cost structure, reducing selling, general and administrative (“SG&A”) expense by 37% year over year. Results also included $9.8 million of non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges following an assessment of asset recoverability in light of lower forecast revenue and operating results. Including these charges, SUNation reported an operating loss of $11.7 million and a net loss of $11.8 million.

SUNation also continued to advance its proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. (“Suniva”). SUNation currently anticipates closing in the first quarter of 2027, subject to satisfaction or waiver of applicable closing conditions and receipt of required approvals and regulatory clearances.

Q3 2026 HIGHLIGHTS

  • Revenue and gross margin improved sequentially
    Revenue increased to $11.2 million from $8.2 million in Q2 2026, and gross margin improved to 30.8% from 26.1%. Revenue declined 41% year over year, primarily reflecting lower residential installation activity.
  • Commercial revenue grew 20% year over year
    Commercial revenue reached $2.66 million, compared with $2.23 million in Q3 2025, primarily driven by growth in New York.
  • SG&A expense declined 37% year over year
    SG&A expense decreased to $4.33 million from $6.90 million, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions.
  • Net loss reflected non-cash impairment charges
    Net loss was $11.82 million, compared with $0.39 million in Q3 2025. Results included $9.82 million of non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges reflecting lower forecast revenue and operating results.
  • Suniva merger process advanced
    The companies amended their merger agreement during the quarter to address financing, stockholder approvals and closing requirements. Closing is currently anticipated in Q1 2027, subject to applicable conditions and approvals.

Commercial Growth Supports Revenue Diversification

The quarter’s sequential revenue and gross-margin improvement occurred within a residential market that continued to operate below prior-year activity levels. Residential revenue declined 52% year over year, while commercial revenue increased 20%. Commercial and service revenue together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue, compared with approximately 18% in Q3 2025.

The prior-year quarter also benefited from residential demand ahead of the year-end 2025 tax credit expiration, contributing to the year-over-year comparison. Management continues to emphasize commercial projects, battery storage, service and adjacent energy offerings as part of its efforts to diversify revenue.

Storage Opportunities Support Adaptation to Residential Market Changes

The expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at year-end 2025 under OBBBA continued to affect residential demand, installation volumes and financing economics during Q3 2026, following elevated activity ahead of the expiration. Lower installation volumes also increased fixed labor and overhead costs as a percentage of revenue.

Battery storage remains an area of focus. Hawaii’s Bring Your Own Device Plus program provides incentives for qualifying customers to add storage to existing or new rooftop solar systems. Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year over year during the quarter.

Updated Asset Values and Liquidity Priorities

The Company’s impairment assessment reflected a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results. Goodwill impairment charges related to the SUNation Residential and SUNation Commercial reporting units, while intangible asset impairment charges related to tradenames and trademarks across the New York and Hawaii businesses.

SUNation continues to prioritize cash preservation, disciplined working capital management and additional financing to support operations and maintain financial flexibility. The Company ended the quarter with $2.79 million in cash and cash equivalents and requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs.

MANAGEMENT COMMENTARY

“Third-quarter revenue and gross margin improved from the second quarter as activity increased across our New York and Hawaii businesses,” said Scott Maskin, Chief Executive Officer of SUNation. “Commercial revenue grew 20% year over year, and commercial and service work represented a larger share of our business. Residential demand continues to reflect the change in customer economics following the expiration of the federal residential tax credit, and our teams remain focused on matching our offerings and operating structure to the market we are serving.”

Mr. Maskin continued, “Our priorities remain disciplined execution, customer service, cost management and liquidity. We are pursuing commercial projects, storage installations, service work, roofing and adjacent energy opportunities while managing expenses closely. We also continued to advance the Suniva merger process during the quarter, including an amendment to the merger agreement addressing financing and closing-related matters.”

James Brennan, SUNation’s Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operations Officer, said, “Higher sequential revenue supported gross-margin improvement to 30.8%, while year-over-year SG&A expense declined 37% following reductions in selling, marketing and personnel costs. Our reported results also included $9.8 million of non-cash impairment charges reflecting the effect of lower forecast revenue and operating results on the carrying value of goodwill and intangible assets.”

Mr. Brennan added, “Cash preservation, working capital management and access to additional capital remain essential. We ended September with $2.8 million of cash and cash equivalents, and our working capital position continues to require close management. We are evaluating financing sources and managing our obligations while supporting customer commitments and the proposed transaction.”

Mr. Maskin concluded, “We currently anticipate completing the Suniva merger in the first quarter of 2027, subject to the required conditions and approvals. Our immediate responsibility is to operate the business carefully through that process, serve our customers and preserve financial flexibility. The experience of our teams in New York and Hawaii, our customer relationships and our range of energy services remain important foundations as we navigate the current market.”

Q3 2026 FINANCIAL AND OPERATIONAL RESULTS

FINANCIAL RESULTS

  • Revenue
    Consolidated revenue was $11.20 million, compared with $18.99 million in Q3 2025, a decrease of 41%. Residential contract revenue declined 52%, partially offset by 20% growth in commercial revenue.
  • Gross profit and margin
    Gross profit was $3.45 million, compared with $7.21 million in Q3 2025. Gross margin was 30.8%, compared with 38.0% in the prior-year quarter, reflecting lower revenue and fixed labor and overhead costs that declined more slowly than sales volume. Gross profit and margin improved sequentially from approximately $2.1 million and 26.1%, respectively, in Q2 2026.
  • Operating expenses and cost reductions
    Total operating expenses were $15.16 million, compared with $7.46 million in Q3 2025, including $9.82 million of non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges and $0.46 million of Suniva merger transaction costs. SG&A expense declined 37% to $4.33 million from $6.90 million, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions.
  • Net loss
    Net loss was $11.82 million, or $1.81 per basic and diluted share, compared with $0.39 million, or $0.12 per basic and diluted share, in Q3 2025. The increase reflected the impairment charges and lower gross profit, partially offset by reduced SG&A expense. Operating loss was $11.71 million, compared with $0.25 million in Q3 2025. Impairment charges comprised $4.92 million of goodwill and $4.90 million of intangible assets. Amortization expense was unchanged year over year at $0.56 million.

For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, revenue was $26.56 million, gross profit was $7.17 million and SG&A expense was $13.87 million, compared with $44.69 million, $16.48 million and $19.38 million, respectively, in the prior-year period. Net loss, including the third-quarter impairment charges, was $19.25 million, compared with $13.50 million in the prior year.

BALANCE SHEET AND LIQUIDITY

The following comparisons are with December 31, 2025, unless otherwise indicated.

  • Cash and working capital
    Cash and cash equivalents were $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, compared with $7.18 million at year-end. The Company had a working capital deficit of $5.35 million, compared with positive working capital of $1.07 million. Net cash used in operating activities during the first nine months of 2026 was $6.54 million, partially offset by $2.11 million of net cash provided by financing activities.
  • Payables and loans payable
    Accounts payable declined 23% to $5.66 million from $7.40 million. The aggregate carrying amount of current and long-term loans payable and related interest, including related-party balances, declined to $4.98 million from $6.60 million, reflecting repayments, the related-party debt conversion completed earlier in 2026 and borrowings under the affiliated revolving credit facility.
  • Credit facility extension
    On October 15, 2026, the maturity of the Company’s $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility was extended to April 15, 2027. Borrowings outstanding were $0.80 million at September 30, 2026, and the Company was in compliance with the facility’s covenants and other requirements at that date.

Total liabilities were $22.78 million, compared with $23.90 million at year-end. Current liabilities increased to $16.96 million from $15.41 million, while long-term liabilities declined to $5.82 million from $8.49 million. Stockholders’ equity was $8.69 million, compared with $24.35 million at year-end and $20.52 million at June 30, 2026, with the sequential decline primarily reflecting the third-quarter net loss, including impairment charges.

The Company requires additional capital resources and is considering all available options, including the ongoing strategic initiatives previously announced. The availability, timing, and terms of any additional funding remains undetermined.

OPERATIONAL RESULTS

  • Residential revenue
    Consolidated residential contract revenue was $7.53 million, compared with $15.66 million in Q3 2025, reflecting lower installation activity in New York and.
  • Commercial revenue
    Consolidated commercial contract revenue increased 20% to $2.66 million from $2.23 million, primarily driven by New York, where commercial revenue increased to $2.63 million from $2.23 million.
  • Service revenue
    Consolidated service revenue was $1.01 million, compared with $1.11 million in Q3 2025. Hawaii service revenue increased 54% to $0.37 million, supported by increased repair and replacement installations, partially offsetting lower New York service revenue.

By operating segment, SUNation NY reported revenue of $8.01 million and gross profit of $2.61 million, compared with $13.01 million and $5.29 million, respectively, in Q3 2025. HEC reported revenue of $3.19 million and gross profit of $0.84 million, compared with $5.98 million and $1.92 million, respectively. Hawaii’s lower residential installation volumes were partially offset by higher price per watt, increased battery attachment rates and service growth.

The Company continues to evaluate product offerings and financing options to support solar and storage adoption while pursuing commercial, service, roofing and adjacent energy opportunities.

STRATEGIC INITIATIVES AND PROPOSED SUNIVA MERGER

SUNation continued to advance its proposed reverse merger with Suniva during Q3 2026. The transaction, announced in June following the Board’s review of strategic alternatives, would result in Suniva becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of SUNation.

On September 4, 2026, the parties amended the merger agreement to address financing arrangements, stockholder approvals and closing requirements. The amendment revised SUNation’s closing net cash requirement to negative $2.5 million, subject to adjustment for potential capital raises, and added a proposed increase in authorized common shares from 1.0 billion to 1.5 billion to the matters requiring stockholder approval.

The amendment also provides for SUNation to use reasonable best efforts to repay or convert into equity up to approximately $2.61 million of specified related-party loans. Any conversion would be at $2.26 per share and subject to stockholder approval (with any related parties abstaining from the vote). These arrangements remain subject to the merger agreement, as amended.

The Company has confidentially submitted a registration statement on Form S-4 containing a proxy statement/prospectus relating to the proposed transaction. Closing remains subject to required stockholder approvals, effectiveness of the registration statement, Nasdaq listing approval and other applicable closing conditions and regulatory clearances. The timing and completion of the transaction remain uncertain.

Alongside the merger process, SUNation continued to manage its capital resources. During the first nine months of 2026, the Company completed a private placement generating approximately $2.7 million in gross proceeds for working capital and general corporate purposes, converted $1.2 million of related-party note principal into equity and made approximately $1.2 million of payments against third-party and related-party loans.

BUSINESS STRATEGY AND OUTLOOK

SUNation’s near-term priorities are to preserve liquidity, manage working capital, align costs with current revenue levels and advance the proposed Suniva merger. Management expects residential demand and installation activity to remain sensitive to customer financing economics and the market’s adjustment to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit.

The Company remains focused on serving customers in New York and Hawaii while diversifying revenue through commercial projects, battery storage, maintenance and repair, roofing and adjacent energy services. Management will continue to evaluate financing alternatives to support operations and maintain financial flexibility as it pursues these priorities.

data.title: S&P 500 Posts Largest Weekly Drop of 2026, Enters Correction Territory
data.description:
04:45 PM EST, 11/20/2026 (MT Newswires) -- The Standard & Poor's 500 index fell 8.6% this week, its largest weekly drop since April 2025, sending the market benchmark into correction territory.

The S&P 500 ended the week at 6,910.39. Friday was the index's seventh consecutive session in the red, marking the longest daily losing streak since February 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic roiled markets.

The week's decline nearly wiped out the S&P 500's year-to-date advance. It is now up by just under 1% for 2026 versus a year-to-date gain of 10% a week earlier.

Technology stocks led the slide amid increasing concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom.

The selloff came even as Anthropic (ANT), maker of the Claude AI chatbot, had a record Nasdaq initial public offering. Anthropic's shares jumped 17% in their Thursday debut before falling 9.1% on Friday.

All of the S&P 500's 11 sectors recorded weekly declines. The technology sector tumbled 12%, followed by a 9.4% loss in communication services, a 7.9% drop in materials, a 7.4% slip in industrials and a 7% drop in energy.

Financials, consumer discretionary and health care shed more than 6% each. Real estate lost 4.3%, utilities declined 3.2% and consumer staples fell 2%.

Sandisk ( SNDK ) had the largest percentage drop in the technology sector as well as the overall S&P 500, sliding 28%.

NVIDIA ( NVDA ) was also hit hard, down 23% on the week. The US Securities & Exchange Commission is looking into the company's accounting practices, Reuters reported Friday, citing two people briefed on the matter. Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA's ( NVDA ) CEO last week following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

Skydance ( SKYD/WS ) had the largest percentage drop in communication services, falling 17%, amid reports the company is combining Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios into a single entity that will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios.

data.title: Nasdaq plunges 5% a day after Anthropic debut, but investors still believe in AI
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Tech stocks slumped on Friday to a 10% weekly decline in the Nasdaq composite, the biggest since 2020, just surpassing the pullback in response to the Liberation Day tariff announcements in spring 2025. 

Nvidia ( NVDA ) tumbled 14% on Friday and 23% for the week after Reuters reported the Securities and Exchange Commission was probing its accounting. Anthropic dropped 9% after earlier falling as much as 14% following its blockbuster IPO, and the semiconductor index of AI favorites fell 11% in a broad retreat from risk. 

For the day, the Nasdaq dropped 5.3%, the S&P 500 fell 3.7% and Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX volatility index, soared 33% to 37. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note fell 12 basis points to 4.93%. 

Even so, investors largely said they continued to believe in the AI trade, which took markets to record highs as recently as last month. 

COMMENTS:

MICHAEL MONAGHAN, PORTFOLIO MANAGER AND PARTNER AT FOUNDER ETFS, DALLAS, TEXAS:

"In the short run, sentiment drives prices. In the long run, fundamentals do. Right now the market is selling first and asking questions later. In our view, the fundamentals remain strong, and we expect prices to reflect them over time."

GENE GOLDMAN, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER AT CETERA, EL SEGUNDO, CA:

"This week's chip earnings were an earnings test, and they passed it. Yesterday's AI IPO is a valuation test, and with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in."

RICHARD SAPERSTEIN, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, TREASURY PARTNERS, NEW YORK:

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth. This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia ( NVDA ) crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.

"Investors are broadly reducing exposure to technology and AI-related equities in favor of non-technology sectors, such as health care, energy and utilities.

"Within technology, we still like the hyperscalers, which can benefit from any slowing data center buildouts since they already own many of them, and cybersecurity, as the recent wave of cyber outages increases demand for their products.

"Investors should maintain long-term allocations to large cap technology stocks, as AI adoption will continue to accelerate and drive economic growth and productivity. A slowdown in AI spending will extend the cycle over a longer time period. In the near term, hyperscaler capital expenditures may begin to slow, giving rise to free cash flow."

MARK HACKETT, CHIEF MARKET STRATEGIST FROM NATIONWIDE FINANCIAL, DOWNINGTOWN, PENNSYLVANIA:

"The current environment is reminiscent of the market action surrounding Liberation Day and the breakout of the conflict with Iran. Those resolved quickly as the reality did not match the fear, with retail investors aggressively buying the dip and indexes returning to record highs within months.

"After months of rotational price action, the recent de-grossing feels as though it has arrived gradually, then suddenly. A capitulatory washout could ultimately prove constructive. If this evolves into a true flush, it may serve as the reset needed to improve positioning, sentiment, and the odds of a more sustainable rally into year-end. The fundamental backdrop remains strong, and sentiment and positioning are supportive from a contrarian standpoint, but picking bottoms is difficult when the market is so emotional."

TIM GHRISKEY, SENIOR PORTFOLIO STRATEGIST AT INGALLS & SNYDER IN NEW YORK:

"Interest rates are going up and we have signs of consumer inflation. The Fed is likely to raise rates at the December meeting and possibly the January meeting as well. Financial markets hate higher interest rates. It's medicine that's often necessary to break down inflation. A lot of the inflation is energy related, oil related, but, that finds its way into various other goods and services.

"In general, you know, we have an increasing interest rate environment. We have for a while, and the market sort of has been ignoring it somewhat but it's out there. Since mid-October when the slide began to happen there's been more awareness of it. Fed speakers have been talking about it more. We've had a lot of Fed speak, especially this week. That's the overriding issue.

"The other issue technology in general and AI. Some of that is valuation related and some is the disruption at Nvdia. It was the largest company in the US market and now it's not. It's had this drama and currently a lack of leadership. It's clear to us that the CFO, who's the interim CEO, as well as keeping her CFO job and everything else, is probably a bit overwhelmed by all of this."

PHILIP PALUMBO, CEO AND CIO, PALUMBO WEALTH MANAGEMENT, NEW YORK:

"In the short term, markets move based on sentiment, emotion, headlines, and investors' opinions about what may happen next. Fear and uncertainty can drive prices lower, sometimes very quickly.

"But over time, what matters most is the underlying value of the businesses we own. Their earnings, cash flow, competitive advantages, and ability to grow ultimately determine their long-term value. That is where our attention remains focused."

JIM AWAD, SENIOR MANAGING DIRECTOR AT CLEARSTEAD ADVISORS LLC IN NEW YORK:

"You have a growth fear in terms of the economy because of the wealth destruction in the stock market, because of fears of moderation in AI spending, and fears that Nvidia ( NVDA ) problems will spread beyond Nvidia ( NVDA ). So you haven't yet seen a significant deceleration in profit estimates for next year. But that would naturally follow if this turbulence continues. But my expectation is that the turbulence will pass, stock prices will recover, and interest rates on balance will be higher over coming months."

LAWRENCE GILLUM, CHIEF FIXED INCOME STRATEGIST AT LPL FINANCIAL, FORT MILL, SOUTH CAROLINA:

"Right now, we think that this is just kind of more technical in nature and not necessarily something that is broadly concerning. We still think that the AI trade has legs. So we think that this is kind of not a bubble bursting, if you will. This is just kind of just some growing concerns, and adding to those concerns is just this time of the year.

"There's a lot of investors out there who are trying to kind of keep their gains for the year. So they're kind of selling now and asking questions later. So that's not really helping. So those are all things that are potentially pushing downward pressure on the equity markets. But that's been a good thing for the Treasury market in terms of that safe haven status.

"The Fed minutes came out this week and suggested that the Fed is pretty unified about higher interest rates. So we still think that that's likely going to happen. One of the things that's helping with the growth and inflation story, at least from the fixed income markets perspective, is if you think about just how much of a tailwind to economic growth the AI capex has been.

"If that slows a little bit, then potentially, economic growth slows a little bit, inflation comes down a little bit, and maybe the Fed doesn't have to hike as aggressively as what markets are pricing in. And in that scenario, that would help Treasury markets as well... It's a little bit more concerning perhaps on the economic growth side, but we don't think recession is in the cards anytime soon."

(Reporting by Chuck Mikolajczak, Sinead Carew, Caroline Valetkevitch, editing by Colin Barr)
